# generator-shortcuts

> For this generator, name the strongest plausible shortcut or rival rule that fits the canonical demonstrations. Give an exact input on which it disagrees with the intended rule, how you checked the output, and whether your proposed generator emits such cases.

## D1: Exact singleton matching with the wrong connectivity

The rival I would prioritize is: **find four-neighbor nonzero components, crop each bounding box, count exact colored crops, and return the first crop occurring once**. It preserves almost all of the intended computation but uses orthogonal connectivity instead of the required eight-neighbor connectivity. This is a plausible segmentation error, not a contrived lookup table. It fits all four canonical train/test pairs. On the baseline protocol it succeeds on 1,731/1,800 inputs (96.17%), so ordinary sample inspection would easily miss it.

The intended rule joins diagonal foreground contacts into the same multicolor object before cropping and counting. No color normalization, reflection normalization, or zero-cell deletion is used.

## Exact emitted counterexample

Seed: `connectivity-census-v1`; sample index **19**; difficulty **easy**; override `pattern_profile="shape_shift"`. Each digit below is one cell, and each line is one row of this exact 13×13 input:

```text
0044000000000
0000400700000
0004408220000
0000007800000
0000000000440
0700000000004
8220000000044
7800400000000
0000404000000
0000044000000
0000000000000
0000000000000
0000000000000
```

Actual Racket output:

```json
[[4, 0, 0], [4, 0, 4], [0, 4, 4]]
```

Four-neighbor rival output:

```json
[[4], [4]]
```

The answer crop is one object under eight-neighbor connectivity but splits under four-neighbor connectivity. Duplicated diagonal objects are also present, so simply choosing a diagonal object is insufficient.

## Verification and emission status

The generator's validator returns `[]` for this input. It lies in the documented domain and **is emitted by the final generator**, not merely accepted by the validator. The independent census derives the intended crop with its own flood fill, then executes the unchanged canonical Racket program through `RacketBridge` and compares the results. `checks/question-counterexample.json` contains the full integer grid, both outputs, source identities, parameters, and command. It is not a masked solve query.

Final generator SHA-256: `8700398dc69b3e155a72ac7624307ec1d312e877cfeab3e7df4bfbfb8482cf57`. Canonical program SHA-256: `640d5deff723c95eb5ee161d578592e7eaac3bf36c965b02a0fc973007837a9b`. Baseline generator SHA-256: `073456bd402dc0c357a80b208fd3afcd1b90e13288583f08e58bd55a333b7f6d`.

Reproduce the retained final census from `packet_root`:

```bash
python3 run_with_racket.py python3 \
  generators/7c2a3ec6c4fb/workspace/connectivity_census.py \
  --samples 1800 --racket --out ../checks/connectivity-after.json
```

This protocol uses indices 0–1799 and 200 samples per difficulty/profile stratum. All 1,800 final inputs are distinct within the run and all labels matched Racket. The final generator emits 593 diagonal counterexamples in this protocol, versus 69 before; `shape_shift` increases from 0/600 to 186/600. A separate default-profile census has 611/1,800 counterexamples, with a different seed/protocol; these are not additional unique training counts.

“Strongest” here means the most concerning new plausible rival found in this review, not an exhaustive ordering of all possible learned shortcuts. The executable rival and its named witness remain in the generator to make future regressions detectable.
